title: U.S. House · Massachusetts's 5th District
area: Middlesex County suburbs north and west of Boston, including Melrose, Malden, Medford, Arlington, Newton and Framingham.

context.text: Incumbent Katherine Clark, the House Democratic Whip, defeated Jonathan Paz and Tarik Samman in the September 1, 2026 Democratic primary. No Republican qualified for the general-election ballot: write-in candidate Walter Grochowski did not receive enough votes in the Republican primary to advance. Clark is unopposed on the November 3 general-election ballot.

candidates.name: Katherine Clark
candidates.ballotNote: Won the September 1, 2026 Democratic primary; unopposed in the general election.

summary.text: Katherine Clark is the incumbent Democratic U.S. Representative for Massachusetts's 5th District and the House Democratic Whip, the second-ranking position in House Democratic leadership. A lawyer by training, she served on the Melrose school committee and in both chambers of the Massachusetts Legislature before winning a 2013 special election to Congress. She is unopposed in the November 3 general election.

background.text: Born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1963 (July 17, according to Wikipedia).
Earned a bachelor's degree in history from St. Lawrence University (1985), a J.D. from Cornell Law School (1989), and an M.P.A. from Harvard's Kennedy School (1997).

Worked as an attorney in Chicago and Colorado before moving to Massachusetts in 1995, where she became General Counsel of the Massachusetts Office of Child Care Services; she later served as policy chief for the Massachusetts Attorney General.

Served on the Melrose, Massachusetts, school committee (2001-2007 per Ballotpedia, including as chair from 2005), and lost a 2004 run for the Massachusetts Senate to Republican incumbent Richard Tisei.

Won a January 2008 special election for the Massachusetts House of Representatives, then won the State Senate seat in the 2010 election and served there until 2013. In the Senate she co-chaired the Joint Committee on Public Service and was lead Senate author of a municipal pension reform bill.
Won the 2013 special election to succeed Ed Markey in the U.S. House and was sworn in on December 12, 2013; she has served on the House Appropriations Committee.

Served as vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus (2019-2021) and Assistant Speaker (2021-2023); elected House Democratic Whip for the 118th Congress in November 2022 and re-elected for the 119th Congress in November 2024, running unopposed both times.
According to her official biography, she lives in Revere with her husband and has three children.

priorities.text: Children and families: says she is fighting for an economy that puts families first.
Reproductive freedom: says the right to decide if and when to have children is fundamental.
Climate change: calls it the existential threat of our time and says it demands an all-hands-on-deck response.

positions.summary: Lists reproductive freedom as a top priority, saying the right to decide if and when to have children is fundamental to a free society.
positions.quote: The right to decide if and when to have children is fundamental to any free society.

positions.summary: Calls the climate crisis the existential threat of our time and calls for an all-hands-on-deck response.
positions.quote: Climate crisis is the existential threat of our time and demands an all-hands-on-deck response.

positions.summary: Says elected officials have a solemn responsibility to address gun violence.
positions.quote: Elected officials have a solemn responsibility to tackle this uniquely American crisis.

positions.summary: Says she believes health care, including reproductive freedom and prescription-drug affordability, is a human right.
positions.quote: From prescription medicine to reproductive freedom, I believe that health care is a human right.

positions.summary: Frames her immigration priority around opportunity rather than enforcement, saying she is committed to the U.S. remaining a beacon of opportunity amid what she calls a rising tide of xenophobia.
positions.quote: Amid a rising tide of xenophobia, I'm committed to ensuring the U.S. remains a beacon of opportunity.

record.text: Assigned to the House Committee on Appropriations, including the Labor, Health and Human Services, Education subcommittee and the Transportation, Housing and Urban Development subcommittee, in the 117th Congress (2021-2022).
Elected House Democratic Whip by House Democrats for the 118th Congress, the second-ranking position in the party's House leadership, running unopposed.
Re-elected House Democratic Whip for the 119th Congress, running unopposed.

researchNotes: Clark is unopposed in the general election; no Republican or third-party candidate qualified for the November ballot. Federal key votes and FEC finance totals are added separately by script. Biography sources disagree on Clark's early legal career (Ballotpedia lists a Colorado Attorney General prosecutor role; Wikipedia lists a federal court clerkship and a Colorado District Attorneys' Council role), so that detail is omitted.
